newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium stocks tumble, alloy down over week.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium stocks tumble, alloy down over week.

text.p: The fall in aluminium stocks to less than 800,000 tonnes, their lowest for over a year, was the feature of this week's London Metal Exchange stock returns.
Traders and analysts said the 11,975 tonne decline over the week reflected good physical demand, which has resulted in sizeable drawdowns from the January 1997 peak of around 968,000 tonnes.
Physical demand in the U.S. remains robust, prompting further moves of aluminium from European warehouses.
LME brokers Brandeis noted that IPAI stocks of unwrought aluminium had fallen by 139,000 tonnes in the first two months of this year to 30 days production and one of the lowest levels for 10 years.
Combined LME and IPAI inventories equate to around six weeks supply.
But some traders, while believing nearby physical demand was strong, were cautious about recent drawdowns, which have seen a 144,050, or 15.10 decline, on January levels.

In a recent report, broker Macquarie Equities said some of the shifting of material from LME warehouses was into financing deals. The wider contango in recent weeks could justify financing metal forward for the period to October/November.
LME brokers Brandeis said unreported stocks held on consignment were still estimated to be in excess of 300,000 tonnes.
Brandies noted that over one million tonnes of aluminium was being held in the form of stocks of scrap, secondary and metal in process at producers.
Aluminium alloy stocks fell again on Friday, with the 260 tonne decline making the total for the week 1,780 tonnes.

Traders said the consistent falls in alloy stocks this year reflected a fundamentally sound market. And this week's decline reflected material being taken out of mostly UK stores destined for the Far East.
"Once it is taken out it cannot be put back in, so it is going to either consumers or producers. If it is a producer they are re-melting it because scrap is in short supply," one said.

Recent trends in the LME alloy market are more encouraging, with business picking up from consumers. This is because end-users have shaken off their worries over material being oxidised after long-term storage.
"If the price is right, they will buy from it (LME)," the trader said.
Recent high backwardations in copper this week reversed a string of declines in LME inventories.
Over the week copper netted a 2,725 tonne gain as metal was attracted to LME warehouses.
Earlier on Monday copper's cash to three months spread was around $200, although this subsequently eased to $75.
Traders said the net gain in copper stocks was factored into the market and a series of sizeable builds would have to be registered for them to reappraise fundamentals.

Zinc stocks fell by 2,525 tonnes on the week, although traders remained wary about Chinese shipments. Nickel stocks fell by 186 tonnes as shipments from the Russian port of Dudinka slowed due to seasonal flooding.
